title: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The fertility of first crosses between species and of their hybrids is largely, though not strictly, governed by systematic affinity, so that species of distinct families never produce hybrids while closely allied species generally cross easily.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Now the fertility of first crosses between species, and of the hybrids produced from them, is largely governed by their systematic affinity.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VIII, “Hybridism”; section “Laws governing the sterility of hybrids”. Scope: interspecific crosses in plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch08-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Standard comparative models can test affinity effects and exceptions. Data coverage supports multiple clade-level analyses but not the full scope across plants and animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress first-cross and hybrid fertility on independently estimated phylogenetic distance across species pairs, allowing clade-specific effects. A strong negative but imperfect relationship supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The categorical family-level assertion is difficult to sample comprehensively.

Cross-outcome data are incomplete and biased toward close relatives.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.66
discriminating power: 0.76
data existence: 0.76
data adequacy: 0.54
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genetic distance is a better independent measure of affinity than a taxonomy that may already have used fertility, and the fly dataset plus public distances make the regression a standard analysis. Discriminating power is high inside the clades that have both variables. Adequacy is only partial because plants, vertebrates, and most invertebrates lack a similarly complete open crossing table.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress first-cross success and hybrid fertility on genetic or phylogenetic distance. A strong positive relationship of isolation with distance, with residual scatter and with no hybrids between families, supports affinity as a large but not strict governor; no relationship, or frequent fertile crosses between distant families, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genetic distance is a proxy for the systematic affinity of 1859 classifications.

Crossing outcomes outside a few model clades are not in the same table as the distances.

Family rank is a human cutoff, so 'never between families' partly reflects how families were drawn.

data adequacy: 0.5

data existence: 0.72
